name: Urim
confidence_why: Luoma 1985, Hemmilä & Luoma's Urim grammar (1987/2009) and Luoma 2000 all place stress on the most open, unreduced vowel of the root (the second of two equally open vowels), but they come from the same fieldworkers, Luoma 1985 calls stress hard to hear and its printed vowel rule is inverted against its own examples, and Wood 2012's second-hand summary ('typically on the final syllable') rewords the rule differently.
catalog_citation: Luoma, Pirkko. 1985. Tentative phonemic statement of Urim. In John M. Clifton (ed.), Five phonological studies (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 31), 101-122. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics. [Rosetta Project scan, archive.org; journal pp. 102-116 only]
catalog_locator: Section 4.3.1 'Stress', pp. 109-112: opening p. 109 (last paragraph) and p. 110; 'vowel harmony' rule p. 110 (last two paragraphs); stress rule and examples p. 111 (first paragraph, example lists, editor's fn 3); secondary stress p. 111 (last paragraph); reduplication p. 112 (first paragraph) (image PDF)
catalog_quote: [p. 109] It has been somewhat difficult to determine what stress is in Urim. Perceived stress seems to be inconsistent, varying with different repetitions of the lexical item. There is a central vowel which never occurs in one-syllable words or in word final syllables. [...] [p. 110] In successive syllables vowels normally go from open to more closed. Any sequence of vowels in which the transition is from an open vowel to a more closed one or in which the vowels are phonemically identical, will result in the first vowel being reduced to [ə]. This "vowel harmony" rule coupled with the following stress rule systematizes the distribution of both the stress and the central vowel. [p. 111] Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root. It is manifested by ±louder, ±longer, ±less ballistic (than the preceding vowel(s)) and -centralized vowel features. It has to have at least two of these features. Thus, neither are phonemic. These rules work within the root. Examples of vowels going from open to more closed: [...] /ka.rek/ ['karek] 'hen, rooster' [...] /a.tok/ ['atok] 'white ant' [...] Examples of words with [ə]: [...] /ten.tar/ [ten'tar] - [tən'tar] 'miserable' [...] /ku.lu/ [ku'lu] - [kə'lu] 'bottom' [...] The "vowel harmony" rule does not apply over morpheme or word boundaries. If the first syllable of a three-syllable word is stressed, the third syllable usually gets a secondary stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not phonemic. Within the root it falls on the first syllable whose vowel is a full (non-reduced) vowel. A 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) reduces the first of two successive vowels to [ə] when the sequence goes from an open vowel to a more closed one or when the two vowels are identical, so such words are stressed on the second syllable (e.g. /ten.tar/ [tənˈtar] 'miserable', /ku.lu/ [kəˈlu] 'bottom'); words whose vowels go from open to more closed are stressed on the first (e.g. /ka.rek/ [ˈkarek] 'hen', /a.tok/ [ˈatok] 'white ant'). Stress is cued by at least two of: louder, longer, less ballistic decay, non-central vowel. The later Hemmilä & Luoma grammar as reported by Wood (2012:7) restates the same distribution from the other end: stress is typically final, always final in verbs, and initial in disyllabic nouns only when the first vowel is more open than the second. the compilers footnote 3 (p. 111) offers exactly that alternative formulation. Reading 'weight-sensitive' is chosen because placement depends on vowel quality (full vs. reduced/central vowel), not on a fixed edge; a catalog user could equally file it as 'fixed: initial syllable with schwa-skipping' or, per Wood/Hemmilä & Luoma, as 'predominantly final'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 111: 'If the first syllable of a three-syllable word is stressed, the third syllable usually gets a secondary stress' (/met-en/ [ˈmetˌen]). p. 112: in reduplicated words 'All parts are stressed; the first one gets the primary stress' (/naŋ-naŋ/ [ˈnaŋˌnaŋ] 'sing-sing').
new_statements.exceptions: Author admits perceived stress is inconsistent across repetitions and that the analyzer did not settle it; a residue of disyllables (longer vowel in 1st syllable, louder in 2nd) did not fit either group. Nearly all disyllabic irrealis verbs have [ə] in the first syllable (hence final stress). Rule does not apply across morpheme or word boundaries (compounds, reduplication). Editor's alternative analysis: stress on the second vowel when more closed than the first, otherwise the first. Wood 2012:7 (Kalpm dialect, citing Hemmilä & Luoma n.d.:10) says verbs are always finally stressed and nouns typically so.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word level: 'These rules work within the root'; the vowel-harmony rule 'does not apply over morpheme or word boundaries'. Data are isolated words in a frame (230 di- and trisyllables) with a suprasegmental analyzer (pitch, length, loudness). Intonation treated separately in 4.3.3.
new_statements.identity_note: Luoma 1985 is a description of Urim proper (glottocode urim1252); its dialect statement is on the missing p. 101, but Luoma and Hemmilä worked on the Yangkolen (main) dialect per Wood 2012:8, so the 1985 data are most likely Yangkolen (Urim 1/2). Wood 2012 describes the Kalpm/Kukwo dialect (Nuku district, Sandaun; ~95% cognate with Yangkolen per Luoma 1992) and reports final stress there, e.g. the language name [uˈrim]. Glottolog lists no separate dialect glottocodes. Glottolog ref 23917 is a corrupted record (Healey & Steinkraus Tifal vocabulary concatenated with Hemmilä 1987 Helsinki MA thesis 'Urimin tematiikkaa', a Finnish-language thesis on Urim thematics) and was not pursued.

new_statements.quote: Stressed vowels are usually longer, louder and less ballistic than the unstressed vowels. (Stress has to have at least two of these features.) Stress is assigned to the word on the basis on the relative height of the vowels involved. The stress is assigned to the vowel in the word that is the most open, or to the second/last vowel if they are equally open. [...] Pitch is not a component of stress but functions independently at the clause level. This makes it somewhat difficult to analyse the stress of words in isolation in Urim. Usually stress falls on the first or second syllable of the word. The suffixes ( –e, -en, etc.) never get stress. [p. 10] [...] Stress is never on the syllable with a reduced vowel. [p. 18] [...] A phonological word can have only one main stress in Urim [p. 106]

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the catalog's existing Luoma 1985 statement ('stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root'; weight-sensitive): under the shared reduction rule the first full vowel is the most open one, so placements coincide. The grammar adds the explicit openness formulation, the equal-openness tie-break (second/last vowel), the suffix exclusion, one main stress per phonological word, and that pitch is not a correlate; it also stresses that stress is hard to hear in isolation. It does not repeat the 1985 secondary-stress remark.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is placed by vowel quality (sonority/openness): the most open vowel of the word is stressed; when the vowels are equally open, the second/last of them is stressed. Because of the vowel-reduction rule (rule 10: a vowel followed by a more open or identical vowel inside the morpheme is reduced to schwa), the stressed vowel is always a full, unreduced vowel, so stress usually lands on the first or second syllable. Suffixes (-e, -en, etc.) are never stressed. Correlates are length and intensity, not pitch (pitch works at clause level). One main stress per phonological word. Examples p. 10: /'atopen/ 'to rejoice', /'talpuk/ 'tree branch', /u'ri:pm/ 'wind', /'tapon/ 'wring' vs irrealis /ti'pon/.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in the grammar (Luoma 1985: 111 says a first-syllable-stressed three-syllable word usually gets secondary stress on the third syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes never take stress; the reduction rule works inside the morpheme only, with a few lexicalised exceptions such as pipa 'if' (p. 11); the vowels /u/ and /o/ do not reduce except sometimes before an identical vowel (p. 18); two nouns or two verbs can be joined under one stress (p. 107); interrogatives and tail-head linkages override normal clause rhythm (p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar (p. 7) describes the main Urim dialect east of the Bongos River, called Yangkolen by the Kukwo people; it notes Kukwo-dialect differences in lexicon and some forms but none in stress. Luoma 1985 and the orthography paper cover the same main dialect. Wood 2012 (already held by the project) works with the Kalpm dialect and cites the grammar for stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Independently confirms the grammar's equal-openness tie-break (stress on the second of two equally open vowels) and the reduction rule that makes the 1985 'first full vowel' and the grammar's 'most open vowel' coincide. Compatible with the catalog reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress section; stress appears only through the reduction rule: a vowel is unstressed and reduced when the next syllable has a more open vowel or one of the same degree of openness, so stress falls on the more open vowel, and on the second of two equally open vowels (e.g. /wulu/ stressed on the second syllable). Onomatopoeic reduplications like /ur.ur/ keep stress on both parts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated (only a secondary-stress symbol ˌ in the symbol key, p. 3).
new_statements.exceptions: Reduction usually works only within a root; onomatopoeic reduplications keep both syllables stressed and unreduced (p. 17); /wulu-wale/ keeps the full vowel by analogy with the second half of the reduplication.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar (p. 7) describes the main Urim dialect east of the Bongos River, called Yangkolen by the Kukwo people; it notes Kukwo-dialect differences in lexicon and some forms but none in stress. Luoma 1985 and the orthography paper cover the same main dialect. Wood 2012 (already held by the project) works with the Kalpm dialect and cites the grammar for stress.

readall_conflicts: No genuine disagreement among the sources opened. Luoma 1985 (catalog) says stress is on the first full-vowel syllable of the root; the grammar says it is on the most open vowel, or the second/last of equally open vowels, and never on a reduced vowel or a suffix; the orthography paper restates the reduction rule with the same equal-openness clause. Under the shared reduction rule these give the same placements. Two presentational discrepancies remain: (a) the printed polarity of the 1985 vowel-harmony rule (already flagged in on verification) is inverted relative to its own examples, while the grammar's rule 10 and the orthography paper have the polarity that matches the examples; (b) Wood 2012: 7 summarises the grammar as 'typically on the final syllable.. in verbs always on the final syllable', which is a stronger claim than the grammar itself makes (the grammar says stress usually falls on the first or second syllable and is on the more open vowel). Luoma 1996 could not be opened, so it cannot be checked.

sources.citation: Wood, Joyce Kathleen. 2012. Valence-increasing strategies in Urim syntax. MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics, Dallas. 180 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.2 Phonology, thesis p. 7 (Kalpm/Kukwo dialect): 'Stress in Urim is typically on the final syllable. In verbs it is always on the final syllable. In some two-syllable nouns, if the first syllable vowel is more open than the vowel in the second syllable, stress is on the first syllable; otherwise, stress on the noun is also on the final syllable (Hemmilä & Luoma n.d.:10). The vowel in unstressed syllables is often reduced to [ə] or [ɨ].' Also p. 70: verbs have final stress, -en suffix takes the stress; p. 89 fn 4: itna 'be.on' stressed finally, initial vowel reduced; language name given…
